title: Kitchen Rules
text:
Dear all,

Please remember these simple rules for the office kitchen. First, wash your cups and plates after you use them. Do not leave them in the sink. Second, write your name on your food before you put it in the fridge. Every Friday at 5 p.m., the cleaner will throw away all food without a name. Third, the coffee machine is for everyone, so please turn it off when you finish. If the machine is broken, tell Linda at the front desk. Do not try to fix it yourself.

Thank you for helping us keep the kitchen clean and nice for everyone.

The Office Team

title: Visiting the City Museum
text:

The museum has three floors. The first floor shows the history of the city. The second floor has paintings by local artists. On the third floor, there is a café with a nice view of the river.

title: Why You Should Stand Up More
text:
Many office workers sit for more than eight hours a day. Research suggests that sitting for long periods can increase the risk of back pain, weight gain and heart problems, even for people who exercise regularly. The good news is that small changes can make a difference.

Experts recommend standing up and moving for a few minutes every half hour. You could take phone calls standing, walk to a colleague's desk instead of sending a message, or use the stairs instead of the lift. Some companies now offer standing desks, but standing all day is not the answer either, as it can cause problems with the legs and feet. The key, doctors say, is to change position often rather than to stay in any single position for too long.

title: Recycling Your Old Phone
text:
Every year, millions of old mobile phones end up in drawers or rubbish bins. This is a problem because phones contain valuable metals such as gold, silver and copper, as well as harmful materials that can damage the soil if they are thrown away with normal waste.

Most phone shops and many supermarkets now accept old phones for recycling, and some will even give you a discount on a new device. Before you hand your phone in, however, make sure you back up your photos and contacts, sign out of all accounts, and reset the phone to its factory settings. This protects your personal data.

Recycling one phone may seem like a small step, but if everyone did it, the amount of mining needed for new devices could fall significantly.

title: Understanding Your Credit Card Statement
text:
Your monthly credit card statement shows all the purchases you made during the billing period, the total amount you owe, and two important numbers: the minimum payment and the payment due date.

Many people pay only the minimum amount because it is easier. However, the rest of the balance is then charged interest, often at a rate of 10 to 15 percent per year. Over time, this can make a small purchase very expensive.

If you can, it is best to pay the full balance before the due date. Setting up automatic payments from your bank account is a simple way to avoid late fees. It is also a good idea to check each item on the statement carefully, because mistakes and unauthorised charges do sometimes happen.

title: A Smarter Way to Learn Words
text:
If you have ever studied a list of new words the night before a test and forgotten most of them a week later, you are not alone. Scientists have known for over a hundred years that we forget new information quickly unless we review it.

A technique called spaced repetition can help. Instead of studying a word many times in one day, you review it after one day, then after three days, then after a week, and so on. Each time you remember the word successfully, the gap before the next review gets longer. Many language apps now use this method automatically.

The idea is simple: reviewing information just before you are about to forget it makes the memory stronger, so you spend less time studying overall.

title: Four-Day Week Trial Results
text:
A six-month trial in which 60 companies moved to a four-day working week without reducing pay has ended, and the results have surprised some critics. According to the researchers, most firms reported that productivity stayed the same or improved slightly, while staff sick days fell by around a third.

Employees said they felt less stressed and had more time for family and exercise. However, the picture was not entirely positive. Several companies in customer-facing industries, such as hospitality, struggled to cover shifts, and a handful returned to a five-day week before the trial ended.

The researchers caution that the participating firms volunteered for the trial and may therefore have been unusually well suited to the change. Larger studies, they argue, are needed before governments consider making such schedules widespread.

title: Security Alert: Phishing Emails
text:
IT has noticed a sharp increase in phishing emails sent to staff over the past week. These messages appear to come from our payroll department and ask recipients to "confirm their bank details" by clicking a link before the end of the month. The link leads to a fake login page that looks almost identical to our real one.

Please be aware that payroll will never ask you to update bank details by email. If you receive such a message, do not click any links or open attachments. Instead, use the "Report Phishing" button in your mail client, which sends the message straight to our security team.

If you have already entered your password on the fake page, change it immediately and contact the IT help desk. Acting quickly greatly reduces the risk of further damage.

title: The Hidden Cost of Free Apps
text:
Most of the apps on our phones are free to download, but that does not mean they cost nothing. Many free apps make money by collecting data about how we use them, where we go and what we buy, and then using it to show targeted advertisements or selling it to third parties.

Privacy laws in many countries now require apps to explain what data they collect and to ask for permission. In practice, however, few users read these long and complicated policies. They simply tap "Accept" to get to the app as quickly as possible.

Experts suggest a few simple habits: review app permissions regularly, switch off location access for apps that do not need it, and delete apps you no longer use. None of these steps will make you invisible online, but together they can noticeably reduce how much information you give away.

title: Microplastics in Drinking Water
text:
Microplastics — tiny pieces of plastic smaller than five millimetres — have been found almost everywhere scientists have looked, from deep oceans to mountain snow. Recent studies have also detected them in both tap and bottled water, with bottled water often containing higher levels, possibly because of the packaging itself.

So far, the World Health Organization has said that the evidence does not show a clear risk to human health at current levels. However, it also notes that research is limited and has called for more studies, particularly on the very smallest particles, which may be able to pass into human tissue.

In the meantime, some researchers suggest that people who are concerned could use a home water filter or avoid heating food in plastic containers, although they stress that these measures have not been proven to reduce health risks.

title: Emergency Funds: Why They Matter
text:
Financial planners often say that the first step towards financial security is not investing but building an emergency fund — money set aside to cover unexpected costs such as medical bills, car repairs or a sudden loss of income.

A common rule of thumb is to save enough to cover three to six months of essential living expenses, including rent, food, utilities and loan repayments. People with irregular incomes, such as freelancers, may need more.

The money should be kept somewhere safe and easy to access, such as a separate savings account, rather than in assets whose value can fall quickly. Keeping it separate from your everyday account also reduces the temptation to spend it. Without such a buffer, people facing an emergency often turn to credit cards or high-interest loans, which can turn a short-term problem into long-term debt.

title: Night Markets Go Cashless
text:
Taiwan's night markets, long associated with cash-only food stalls, are gradually embracing mobile payments. In several major cities, local governments have offered small subsidies to vendors who install QR code payment systems, and the share of stalls accepting digital payments has risen steadily over the past three years.

Supporters say the change makes life easier for tourists, who often lack local currency, and reduces the time vendors spend handling change. Some older vendors, however, remain reluctant. They worry about transaction fees, which can reach 2% of each sale, and prefer the simplicity of cash.

Analysts expect the trend to continue, but say cash is unlikely to disappear from night markets any time soon, given its popularity among both older shoppers and vendors.

qs.q: What is the passage mainly about?
qs.a: The slow shift towards mobile payments at night markets
d: Why tourists avoid night markets
A new law that will ban cash payments at all night markets in Taiwan
The history of Taiwanese street food
qs.ex: 夜市逐漸接受行動支付。

qs.q: Why are some vendors unwilling to accept mobile payments?
qs.a: They do not want to pay transaction fees.
d: They are not able to get the subsidies offered by local governments.
Tourists do not use them.
QR codes are illegal at night markets.
qs.ex: 部分攤商擔心最高 2% 的手續費。

qs.q: The word "reluctant" is closest in meaning to:
qs.a: unwilling
d: excited
unable
confused
qs.ex: reluctant = 不情願的。

title: Sleep and Screen Time
text:
Many people check their phones in bed, but a growing body of research suggests this habit may be harming their sleep. Screens emit blue light, which can suppress melatonin, the hormone that signals to the body that it is time to sleep. Perhaps more importantly, scrolling through news or social media keeps the brain alert, making it harder to relax.

Sleep specialists generally recommend stopping screen use at least 30 to 60 minutes before bed. Night mode settings, which reduce blue light, may help a little, but they do not address the problem of mental stimulation.

Instead, experts suggest building a short routine that signals the end of the day, such as reading a paper book, stretching or listening to calm music. Keeping the phone outside the bedroom altogether is one of the most effective changes people can make.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
qs.a: Using screens before bed can harm sleep, and there are ways to reduce this.
d: Night mode completely solves sleep problems.
Melatonin is harmful to the body.
Reading on a phone is better than reading a book.
qs.ex: 睡前用螢幕影響睡眠,並提出改善方法。

qs.q: According to the passage, why is night mode not a full solution?
qs.a: It does not stop the brain from being stimulated.
d: It increases blue light.
It is only available on new phones, so most people cannot use it.
It reduces melatonin.
qs.ex: 夜間模式只減藍光,無法解決大腦被刺激的問題。

qs.q: What does "suppress" mean in the first paragraph?
qs.a: reduce or stop
d: increase
measure
produce
qs.ex: suppress melatonin = 抑制褪黑激素。

title: The Productivity Paradox
text:
Economists have long puzzled over what has become known as the productivity paradox: despite enormous investment in digital technology, measured productivity growth in many advanced economies has been disappointingly sluggish. Several explanations have been proposed.

One holds that official statistics simply fail to capture the value of free digital services, such as search engines and maps, which do not appear in GDP. Another argues that new technologies take decades to reshape how firms are organised; electricity, after all, did not transform factory output until managers redesigned production around it. A third, more pessimistic, view contends that recent innovations are inherently less transformative than earlier ones.

If the second explanation is correct, the recent wave of artificial intelligence may yet deliver substantial gains — but only once organisations have done the slow, unglamorous work of restructuring around it.

qs.q: What is the passage mainly concerned with?
qs.a: Possible reasons why technology has not clearly boosted productivity
d: Proof that digital technology reduces productivity
A history of electricity in factories
How to measure GDP accurately
qs.ex: 探討科技投資未明顯提升生產力的可能原因。

qs.q: Why does the writer mention electricity?
qs.a: To show that the benefits of a technology can take a long time to appear
d: To argue that older inventions like electricity were more important than AI
To explain how GDP is calculated
To criticise factory managers
qs.ex: 以電力為例說明新技術需長時間重組組織才見效。

qs.q: What is implied by "unglamorous" in the final sentence?
qs.a: The necessary changes are slow and not exciting.
d: The changes will be expensive and risky.
AI is less impressive than people think.
Organisations will refuse to change.
qs.ex: unglamorous = 不光鮮、不吸引人的苦工。

title: Rethinking the Open-Plan Office
text:
Open-plan offices were once hailed as a way to break down hierarchies and encourage spontaneous collaboration. The reality has proved more complicated. A widely cited study that tracked employees moving from cubicles to an open layout found that face-to-face interaction actually fell by around 70%, while email and instant messaging rose sharply. Faced with constant visibility and noise, workers appear to have retreated behind headphones and screens.

This does not mean a return to closed offices is inevitable. Many firms are now experimenting with "activity-based" designs that combine quiet zones for focused work, bookable rooms for meetings, and shared spaces for informal conversation. The underlying lesson is perhaps that collaboration cannot simply be engineered by removing walls; it depends on giving people meaningful choices about how and where they work.

qs.q: What is the writer's main point?
qs.a: Removing walls alone does not create collaboration; workers need choice.
d: Open-plan offices should be banned.
Closed offices are always more productive.
Headphones should not be allowed at work.
qs.ex: 單靠拆牆無法促進合作,要給員工選擇。

qs.q: What did the study find after employees moved to an open layout?
qs.a: They talked face to face much less.
d: They sent fewer emails and messages because they could see each other.
They became more creative.
They asked for more meetings.
qs.ex: 面對面互動下降約 70%,電子溝通增加。

qs.q: In the first paragraph, "retreated" most nearly means:
qs.a: withdrew to protect themselves
d: advanced confidently
resigned from their jobs
complained formally
qs.ex: retreated behind headphones = 躲進耳機裡自我隔離。

title: Inflation and Your Savings
text:
When inflation is low, few savers pay much attention to it. Yet even moderate inflation steadily erodes the purchasing power of money held in cash. If prices rise by 3% a year while a savings account pays 1%, the saver is, in real terms, becoming roughly 2% poorer each year, even though the balance on the statement keeps growing.

This distinction between nominal and real returns is easy to overlook, partly because people tend to think about money in face-value terms — a tendency economists call "money illusion". It also explains why the same interest rate can feel generous in one decade and meagre in another.

None of this means that cash has no place in a household's finances; liquidity and stability have genuine value, particularly for emergencies. But understanding real returns allows people to judge more accurately what their savings are actually worth over time.

qs.q: What is the main purpose of the passage?
qs.a: To explain how inflation affects the real value of savings
d: To persuade readers to stop saving cash
To predict future inflation rates
To recommend a particular savings account
qs.ex: 說明通膨如何侵蝕存款實質價值。

qs.q: What does "money illusion" refer to?
qs.a: Thinking about money in face-value rather than real terms
d: Believing that inflation will always be low
Hiding money from the tax authorities by keeping it in cash at home
Expecting banks to pay high interest
qs.ex: money illusion = 以面額而非實質購買力看待金錢。

qs.q: Which statement would the writer most likely agree with?
qs.a: Holding some cash is sensible, as long as you understand its real return.
d: Cash should never be kept at home or in a bank.
Nominal returns are more important than real returns.
A growing account balance always means growing wealth.
qs.ex: 作者肯定現金流動性的價值,但要理解實質報酬。

title: The Case for Boring Infrastructure
text:
Few politicians win elections by promising to replace water pipes. New bridges and stadiums make better photographs, and the benefits of maintenance are, by their nature, invisible: when a pipe is repaired in time, nothing happens. Yet engineers have long argued that neglecting existing infrastructure is one of the most expensive mistakes a government can make.

The reasoning is straightforward. A road resurfaced at the right moment may last another fifteen years; the same road left to crumble can require complete reconstruction at several times the cost. Deferred maintenance, in other words, is not a saving but a loan, and an unusually expensive one.

Some cities have responded by publishing an annual "maintenance gap" — the difference between what should be spent to keep assets in good condition and what is actually spent. Making the gap public does not fix a single pipe, but it turns an invisible problem into a figure that voters and journalists can follow.

qs.q: Why, according to the writer, is maintenance politically unattractive?
qs.a: Its successes are largely invisible.
d: It is always more expensive than new projects.
Engineers disagree about its value.
Voters prefer lower taxes to repairs.
qs.ex: 保養做得好就「什麼事都沒發生」,看不到成果。

qs.q: What does the writer mean by calling deferred maintenance "a loan"?
qs.a: Postponing repairs creates larger costs later.
d: Governments borrow money to pay for repairs.
Repairs should be paid for by private lenders.
Maintenance budgets are usually repaid within a year.
qs.ex: 現在不修 = 以後付更多,像高利貸款。

qs.q: What is the main benefit of publishing a "maintenance gap"?
qs.a: It makes the problem easier for the public to track.
d: It immediately reduces repair costs.
It replaces the need for engineers' reports.
It guarantees more funding for maintenance.
qs.ex: 公布數字讓選民和記者看得到、追得了。

title: Why Meetings Expand
text:
Most office workers can recall a meeting that could have been an email. What is less obvious is why such meetings persist even in organisations that complain about them constantly. One explanation is that meetings serve purposes other than the ones written on the agenda. They allow people to demonstrate commitment, to share responsibility for difficult decisions, and to avoid being blamed later for not having been consulted.

Seen this way, a long invitation list is not simply inefficiency; it is a form of insurance. Each additional attendee slightly reduces the risk that someone will later object that they were left out. The cost of that insurance, however, is paid in hours by everyone in the room.

Companies that have successfully cut meetings rarely do so by banning them. Instead, they change what counts as being consulted — for instance, by circulating a short written proposal with a clear deadline for objections, after which silence is treated as agreement.

qs.q: What is the writer's main point about unnecessary meetings?
qs.a: They continue because they fulfil hidden social functions.
d: They exist mainly because managers enjoy them.
They are rarer than most workers believe.
They can be eliminated by a simple ban.
qs.ex: 會議還有表態、分攤責任、避免被怪的隱藏功能。

qs.q: In what sense is a long invitation list "a form of insurance"?
qs.a: It protects against later complaints of not being included.
d: It ensures that decisions are always correct.
It allows the company to claim back costs.
It guarantees that someone will take notes.
qs.ex: 多邀人,之後比較不會有人抱怨沒被諮詢。

qs.q: Which approach does the writer suggest works better than banning meetings?
qs.a: Redefining consultation through written proposals and deadlines.
d: Limiting meetings to senior managers only.
Making all meetings shorter than fifteen minutes.
Recording meetings for those who cannot attend.
qs.ex: 改用書面提案 + 異議期限,沉默即同意。

title: The Limits of Self-Tracking
text:
Wearable devices now record our steps, heart rate and sleep with impressive precision. It is tempting to assume that more data must lead to better decisions about our health. The evidence, however, is more mixed. Studies of fitness trackers have found that many users stop wearing them within months, and that simply knowing one's step count does not reliably change behaviour.

Part of the problem is that data without interpretation can be confusing or even counterproductive. A sleep score that drops after a stressful day may make some users anxious, which in turn makes sleep worse — a phenomenon researchers have begun to call "orthosomnia".

This does not make the devices useless. They appear most helpful when they are tied to a specific goal, such as training for a race, and when the numbers are treated as rough guides rather than verdicts. The device, in short, works best as a tool for a decision the user has already made.

qs.q: What does the writer suggest about the link between health data and behaviour?
qs.a: Having more data does not automatically change what people do.
d: People who track data are always healthier.
Most trackers give inaccurate readings.
Behaviour changes only when data is shared online.
qs.ex: 知道步數不一定會改變行為。

qs.q: What is "orthosomnia" as described in the passage?
qs.a: Sleep problems made worse by worrying about sleep data.
d: A medical condition caused by wearing devices at night.
The habit of sleeping with a phone nearby.
A method of improving sleep using trackers.
qs.ex: 因為睡眠分數焦慮,反而睡更差。

qs.q: According to the writer, when are trackers most useful?
qs.a: When they support a clear goal and are read as rough guides.
d: When they are worn every day without exception.
When users check their scores as often as possible.
When doctors review the data every week.
qs.ex: 有明確目標、把數字當參考時最有用。

title: Remote Work and the Junior Employee
text:
The debate about remote work is often framed as a contest between flexibility and productivity. For experienced employees, the evidence suggests that working from home costs little and may even help. For people at the start of their careers, the picture is less reassuring.

Much of what junior staff learn is never formally taught. They overhear how a colleague handles a difficult client, notice how a manager structures a proposal, and pick up the unwritten rules of the organisation. Researchers sometimes call this "tacit knowledge", and it travels poorly over video calls, which tend to be scheduled, short and focused on immediate tasks.

Some firms have tried to compensate by asking senior staff to come into the office on the same days as their newest colleagues. The logic is that the benefit of being in the office depends less on the building than on who else is in it. An empty office, after all, teaches nothing.

qs.q: Why might remote work be harder for junior employees?
qs.a: They miss informal learning that happens around colleagues.
d: They are usually less productive at home.
They have less suitable equipment at home.
They are more likely to be monitored.
qs.ex: 新人很多東西靠在旁邊聽、看學到,遠端學不到。

qs.q: Why does tacit knowledge "travel poorly" over video calls?
qs.a: Calls are usually planned, brief and task-focused.
d: Video quality is often too low.
Senior staff refuse to use video calls.
Tacit knowledge must be written down first.
qs.ex: 視訊多半排好、短、只談眼前任務。

qs.q: What does the final sentence imply?
qs.a: Office time is valuable mainly because of the people present.
d: Offices should be closed to save money.
Junior staff should work alone to focus.
Office buildings need better design.
qs.ex: 辦公室的價值在於有誰在,不是建築本身。

title: The Return of the Repair Shop
text:
For decades, the economics of household goods pointed in one direction: it was usually cheaper to replace a broken toaster than to fix it. Labour was expensive, spare parts were hard to find, and many products were designed in ways that made opening them difficult without damaging them.

That calculation is beginning to shift. Several governments have introduced "right to repair" rules requiring manufacturers to make spare parts and repair manuals available for a number of years after a product is sold. Supporters argue that this will reduce waste and give consumers more control over the things they own.

Manufacturers have raised concerns about safety and the protection of their designs, and it remains unclear how many consumers will actually choose repair over replacement. Still, the rules change the default. When repair becomes a realistic option rather than a theoretical one, the decision to throw something away becomes a choice rather than a necessity.

qs.q: Why was replacing goods traditionally cheaper than repairing them?
qs.a: Labour costs, scarce parts and hard-to-open designs.
d: Governments taxed repair services heavily.
New products were always of higher quality.
Consumers preferred the latest models.
qs.ex: 人工貴、零件難找、設計很難拆。

qs.q: What do "right to repair" rules require?
qs.a: Manufacturers must supply parts and manuals for some years.
d: Consumers must repair goods before replacing them.
Shops must offer free repairs for a year.
Products must be designed to last longer.
qs.ex: 製造商要在一段時間內提供零件和維修手冊。

qs.q: What is the writer's overall view of the rules?
qs.a: Their effect is uncertain, but they make repair a real option.
d: They will certainly end the throwaway culture.
They mainly benefit manufacturers.
They are unnecessary because repair is already cheap.
qs.ex: 效果未定,但讓「修」變成真的選項。

title: How Headlines Shape What We Remember
text:
Most readers skim far more articles than they read in full. As a result, the headline often becomes the main thing a reader takes away from a story. Psychologists have shown that a misleading headline can colour how people remember the article beneath it, even when the article itself is accurate and the reader has read it carefully.

In one set of experiments, participants read identical news stories under different headlines. Those whose headline emphasised a minor detail were more likely to recall that detail later and to interpret the rest of the story in its light. The effect was strongest when the headline was subtly slanted rather than obviously false, presumably because readers did not notice anything to correct.

The practical lesson for readers is modest but useful: treat a headline as a claim to be checked against the article rather than as a summary of it. For editors, the findings are a reminder that accuracy in the body of a story does not excuse imprecision at the top.

qs.q: Why do headlines have such a strong influence?
qs.a: Many readers only skim and remember the headline.
d: Headlines are usually written by experts.
Readers trust headlines more than articles.
Articles are often too long to understand.
qs.ex: 多數人只掃標題,標題成了主要記憶。

qs.q: When was the headline effect strongest?
qs.a: When the headline was slightly slanted, not clearly false.
d: When the headline was completely untrue.
When readers skipped the article entirely.
When the article contained errors.
qs.ex: 微妙偏頗比明顯錯誤更有影響,因為讀者沒察覺要修正。

qs.q: What does the writer advise readers to do?
qs.a: Check the headline's claim against the article itself.
d: Stop reading news websites.
Read only the headlines to save time.
Trust articles more than their headlines in every case.
qs.ex: 把標題當成要查證的主張,不是摘要。
